meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The brain is a wonderful organ. It starts working the moment you get up in the morning and does not stop until you get into the office'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Robert Frost. The joke was unsigned magazine filler by 1929 — credited to house organs, never to the poet. No Frost source has ever been located.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — an anonymous office joke
answer.authorDates: In print, credited to no person, by January 1929
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this line under Unsourced on its Robert Frost talk page ↗, where the editor who went looking for it reported he could find no source and instead traced the joke to three 1929 periodicals — The Clerk (January 1929), Country Teacher (September 1929) and The Churchman — two of which credit the trade magazines Telephone Topics and Hardware Age rather than any person. Nothing ties the sentence to a Frost poem, essay, letter or interview, and it appears nowhere in Wikiquote’s sourced Frost quotations ↗.

source.excerpt: The brain is a wonderful organ. It starts working the moment you get up in the morning and does not stop until you get into the office.
trail: Wikiquote’s Robert Frost page ↗ lists his sourced quotations, each tied to a poem, essay or interview. This line is not among them, in any section.

It sits instead on the talk page ↗ under the heading Unsourced. The editor who logged it, R. S. Shaw, wrote on 18 August 2024 that he doubted it was Frost and had found no source, and listed three 1929 periodicals that printed it: The Clerk (vol. 21, January 1929, p. 28), Country Teacher (vol. 11, no. 74, September 1929, p. 66) and The Churchman (vol. 139, 1929, p. 18). Country Teacher credits Telephone Topics; The Churchman credits Hardware Age; The Clerk names no source.

A full-text sweep of Open Library’s scanned books ↗ returns about 490 hits, and the ones that surface are joke anthologies and desk-humour collections — Work and Other Occupational Hazards, The Bathroom Inspiration Book, 101 Reasons Not To Do Anything — rather than anything by Frost.
Quote Investigator ↗, which normally settles questions like this one, has no article on the line at all; its only “wonderful organ” entry concerns a different brain joke.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show. The Wikiquote editor who located the 1929 appearances describes it in each case as a humorous item — a stand-alone squib, not part of a longer piece — and everything since is quotation-book and anthology reprinting.
source.rightsNote: Uncertain — no rights claim can honestly be made. Neither an author nor a first publication can be established: the earliest printings located are 1929 magazine filler that credits other magazines, and the Wikiquote editor who found them argues the line is older still. Because there is no identifiable work or author to date, quotle.info asserts no copyright status here, and no public-domain claim either.

author.name: Robert Frost
author.kicker: The name the joke landed on
author.heading: About Robert Frost
author.metaLine: 1874–1963 · American poet · four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry
author.bio: Robert Frost was born in San Francisco on 26 March 1874 and died on 29 January 1963, and he is the poet of rural New England — Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, Fire and Ice, Home Burial — with four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry to his name. He was famous enough by the end of his life to read The Gift Outright at John F. Kennedy’s inauguration in January 1961, and famous enough afterwards to attract other people’s one-liners. This office gag is one of them. It was already loose in the 1929 periodical press as unsigned filler while Frost was alive, credited to other magazines rather than to him.

misattribution.heading: Where the Frost credit comes from
misattribution.intro: This is a workplace gag that acquired a poet. Every popular source that credits Robert Frost credits him by name alone — no book, no lecture, no letter, no date.

items.why: Goodreads ↗ carries the line under Frost’s name with 287 likes and no citation at all, directly above its own notice that community-added quotes are not verified. That is the shape of the credit everywhere it appears.
Zen Pencils built an illustrated comic ↗ around the line under Frost’s name, again with no source given. Illustrated, shareable versions are how a bare name-only credit hardens into an apparent fact.

The 1929 printings ↗ credit Telephone Topics and Hardware Age — magazines, not people. Neither credit names an author, and reprinting an unsigned squib from another trade paper is exactly how filler travelled.

Frost was alive and well known in 1929, so the date alone does not rule him out. What rules against him is that those 1929 items credit magazines rather than Frost, and that nobody has produced a Frost poem, essay, letter or interview containing the sentence — it is absent from Wikiquote’s sourced Frost quotations ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote it. It was already loose in 1929 periodicals as an unsigned joke, credited to the trade papers Telephone Topics and Hardware Age and to no person — see the Wikiquote record ↗. Frost’s name was attached later, and no one has ever shown where.

context.heading: How a filler joke got a poet’s name
lead: Famous names work like drains. A good line with no owner rolls downhill until it reaches someone big enough to hold it, and for a dry, plain-spoken American epigram of the twentieth century, Robert Frost is about as big as the drain gets. The joke itself is pure office humour — the kind of item a staff newsletter runs in a box to fill a column — and the 1929 magazines that printed it treated it exactly that way: unsigned, reprinted from another magazine, filler.

What makes the Frost credit sticky is that it is almost plausible. Frost really did talk in short, deflating sentences, and he really was quotable. But quotability is not evidence. The test is whether anyone can point to the page, and in nearly a century of quotation books nobody has — the credit travels as a bare name with no book, no lecture, no date behind it.
detailsBody: Two things would close the question. The first is a printing earlier than January 1929 — the Wikiquote editor who assembled the 1929 evidence believes one exists, precisely because those 1929 items are themselves reprints crediting other magazines. The second is any Frost source at all: a poem, a letter, a lecture transcript, a reporter’s notebook. Until one of those turns up, the honest way to use the line is the way its first printers used it — without a name attached.
context.pull: The 1929 printings credit two magazines. Neither of them is a person.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Talk:Robert Frost page lists this line under the heading "Unsourced", where editor R. S. Shaw wrote on 18 August 2024 that he doubts it is Frost, has found no source, and that it predates 1929 because it appears as a humorous item in 1929 periodicals: Country Teacher v.11 Sept 1929 #74 p.66 (giving source as Telephone Topics), The Clerk Vol XXI January 1929 p.28 (London: National Union of Clerks and Administrative Workers), and The Churchman Vol 139 p.18 (1929, giving source as Hardware Age).
The quote does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote's main Robert Frost article — not in the Sourced, Attributed, Misattributed or Disputed sections.

Robert Frost was born 26 March 1874 in San Francisco and died 29 January 1963; he won four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry and read "The Gift Outright" at John F. Kennedy's inauguration on 20 January 1961. The page does not mention any "brain is a wonderful organ" quip.
Goodreads displays the quote credited to Robert Frost with 287 likes, gives no book, publication date or source, and carries a notice that community-added quotes are not verified by Goodreads.
Zen Pencils published an illustrated comic built around this quote credited to Robert Frost, with no source given for the quote.

Open Library's Search Inside returns about 490 full-text results for the phrase "brain is a wonderful organ", and the surfaced titles are modern joke and desk-humour anthologies (e.g. "Work and other occupational hazards", "The Bathroom Inspiration Book", "101 Reasons Not To Do Anything"), not works by Robert Frost.

A Quote Investigator site search for "wonderful organ" returns only one article — about a different joke ("I Thought the Brain Was the Most Important Organ Until I Realized What Was Telling Me That") — confirming QI has not investigated the Robert Frost "until you get into the office" line.
